reader.title: Threatened lynching of Spain at Newberry, South Carolina
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: No one was hurt; the episode consisted of an armed pursuit, threats of lynching and a foiled plan to take a white prisoner from jail and whip him (A1).
Only one local report, the Newberry Herald item, was found (A1).

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Spain at Newberry, South Carolina, took place in February 1882, when a white traveling seed seller accused of insulting a planter's wife was pursued, jailed and threatened by local men.
A sheriff's guard foiled a plan to take him from jail and whip him, and a trial justice ordered him released.
According to the Newberry Herald, the man had been traveling through the county selling garden seed and was in No. 6 Township on Thursday, 9 February.
The paper said he went to a plantation house while the owner was away, insulted the owner's wife at the door and followed her inside.
She fled to the house of a nearby Black family, the paper's "colored family," and the man left.
The husband and some neighbors set out after him early Friday, and the Herald remarked that "had they caught him he would have fared badly."

After riding about fifty miles they turned back and telegraphed to Laurens, where he was arrested and brought by train to jail on Saturday; he gave his name as Spain, of Buncombe County, North Carolina.
On Saturday there were "threats of lynching," which the paper said subsided when "wise counsels prevailed."
On Monday evening word spread that Spain would be taken from the jail and, as the Herald understood it, given "a decent threshing" and turned loose.
The Sheriff learned of the plan and called out a posse to guard the jail, and the crowd dispersed.
Once things were quiet, Trial Justice Fair, on whose warrant Spain had been committed, sent the Sheriff an order of release.
Spain left "at the top of his speed" and, by the paper's account, had not been heard from since; no report of a trial or of charges against those who threatened him appears in the coverage.
The only report found is a local item in the Newberry Herald of 16 February 1882, headed "A Rare Villain."
It treated the accusation as established and named none of the men who pursued or threatened Spain, but credited "wise counsels" and the Sheriff's guard with keeping the peace.

accounts.label: Local newspaper
accounts.gist: The Newberry Herald told the story from the side of the woman's family, called Spain 'A Rare Villain', and reported the lynching threats and foiled jail plan without naming anyone involved.

framing.detail: The headline 'A Rare Villain' and remarks that the husband was 'of course, very angry' treat the accusation as fact, while the paper credits 'wise counsels' and the Sheriff's guard for preventing mob action.
